text: Genes assigned to fitness modules were 86.0% core, versus 81.5% of all genes, a difference of +4.5 percentage points.
quote: - **Module genes: 86.0% core** vs all genes: 81.5% (+4.5 percentage points)
heading: Module Genes Are More Core Than Average

text: The report describes ICA module genes as co-regulated functional units that skew toward the conserved core genome.
quote: - Genes assigned to ICA modules are co-regulated functional units, and they skew toward the conserved core genome
heading: Module Genes Are More Core Than Average

text: Figure reference: Module Core Distribution, figures/module_core_distribution.png.
quote: ![Module Core Distribution](figures/module_core_distribution.png)
heading: Module Genes Are More Core Than Average

text: Among 974 modules with >=3 mapped genes, 577 (59%) were classified as core (>90% core genes), 349 (36%) as mixed (50-90% core), and 48 (5%) as accessory (<50% core).
quote:
Of 974 modules with >=3 mapped genes:
- **577 (59%) are core modules** (>90% core genes)
- 349 (36%) are mixed modules (50-90% core)
- **48 (5%) are accessory modules** (<50% core)
heading: Most Modules Are Core

text: The median module was 93.4% core.
quote: The median module is 93.4% core. Most co-regulated fitness response units are embedded in the conserved genome.
heading: Most Modules Are Core

text: Module-family breadth across organisms did not predict core fraction (Spearman rho=-0.01, p=0.914).
quote: Surprisingly, module families spanning more organisms do NOT have higher core fractions (Spearman rho=-0.01, p=0.914).
heading: Family Breadth Does NOT Predict Conservation

text: The report notes that families were nearly all core regardless of breadth and proposes the high core-genome baseline (~82%) as a reason a gradient may be hard to detect.
quote: Families are nearly all core regardless of how many organisms they span. The core genome baseline is so high (~82%) that there's little room for a gradient.
heading: Family Breadth Does NOT Predict Conservation

text: Figure reference: Family Breadth vs Conservation, figures/family_breadth_vs_conservation.png.
quote: ![Family Breadth vs Conservation](figures/family_breadth_vs_conservation.png)
heading: Family Breadth Does NOT Predict Conservation

text: There were 38 module families with <50% core genes. The proposed explanations—horizontal transfer or niche-specific operons—are hypotheses, not established identities.
quote: 38 families have <50% core genes -- these are co-regulated accessory gene modules conserved across organisms. They may represent horizontally transferred functional units or niche-specific operons.
heading: Accessory Module Families Exist

text: No essential genes appeared in any module (0); the report attributes this exclusion to the absence of transposon-insertion fitness data for essential genes.
quote: 0 essential genes appear in any module, confirming that ICA modules only capture genes with measurable fitness variation (non-essential genes with transposon insertions). Essential genes are invisible to ICA because they have no fitness data.
heading: Essential Genes Are Absent from Modules

text: Core-gene enrichment in ICA fitness modules was reported as 86% versus an 81.5% baseline (OR=1.46, p=1.6e-87).
quote: ICA fitness modules are enriched in core genes (86% vs 81.5% baseline, OR=1.46, p=1.6e-87), confirming that co-regulated functional units preferentially reside in the conserved genome.
heading: Interpretation

text: Fitness Browser is the named data source; the report credits Price et al. (2018) with generating its data and developing the ICA decomposition approach used here.
quote: - **Price et al. (2018)** generated the Fitness Browser data and developed the ICA decomposition approach used to identify co-regulated fitness modules.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report cites Saelens et al. (2018) as literature support for ICA relative to other microbial gene-expression decomposition methods; this is not a result measured in this project.
quote: - **Saelens et al. (2018)** demonstrated that ICA outperforms other decomposition methods for microbial gene expression data, supporting the biological relevance of the modules analyzed here.
heading: Literature Context

text: The report relates its finding that 59% of fitness modules are >90% core to core/accessory-genome definitions reviewed by Vernikos et al. (2015).
quote: - **Vernikos et al. (2015)** reviewed core and accessory genome definitions in bacterial pangenomics. Our finding that 59% of fitness modules are >90% core extends the concept of "core" from individual genes to functionally coherent regulatory units.
heading: Literature Context

text: A baseline core rate of ~81.5% limits observable enrichment; the statistically significant +4.5pp difference to 86% is modest in absolute terms.
quote: - **Ceiling effect**: The baseline core rate is already ~81.5%, limiting the maximum observable enrichment. The +4.5pp difference to 86% is statistically significant but represents a modest absolute effect.
heading: Limitations

text: The conservation analysis covered a 29/32-organism subset: Cola, Kang, and SB2B lacked pangenome links because their species had too few genomes in GTDB for pangenome construction. GTDB is a named dataset.
quote: - **29/32 organism subset**: 3 module organisms (Cola, Kang, SB2B) lack pangenome links because their species had too few genomes in GTDB for pangenome construction.
heading: Limitations

text: Upstream ICA membership required |Pearson r| >= 0.3 and allowed at most 50 genes per module; these choices could affect measured conservation composition.
quote: - **Module membership threshold**: The upstream ICA module membership uses |Pearson r| >= 0.3 with max 50 genes per module. This threshold affects which genes are "in" a module and could influence conservation composition.
heading: Limitations

text: The 90% and 50% cutoffs used to classify core, mixed, and accessory modules were convenient rather than biologically motivated.
quote: - **Classification thresholds are arbitrary**: The 90% and 50% cutoffs for core/mixed/accessory module classification are convenient but not biologically motivated.
heading: Limitations

text: Because ICA requires fitness data, the modules capture only the non-essential portion of the genome.
quote: - **Essential genes excluded**: ICA requires fitness data, so essential genes (no transposon insertions) are absent from all modules. This means modules only capture the non-essential portion of the genome.
heading: Limitations
